source.title: Safetywashing: Do AI Safety Benchmarks Actually Measure Safety Progress?
source.authors: Richard Ren; Steven Basart; Adam Khoja; Alexander Pan; Alice Gatti; Long Phan; Xu-Wang Yin; Mantas Mazeika; Gabriel Mukobi; Ryan Kim; Stephen Fitz; Dan Hendrycks

record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes correlations between model capabilities, training compute, and safety-benchmark scores, but it does not measure held-out pretraining loss, fit or test scaling laws, compare predictions with larger runs, or examine compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports many safety-benchmark correlations with capabilities or compute. Those results do not measure the loss-scaling claims in V1–V7. The two rows record its separate measurements of capability-score versus training-compute correlations; these are related to scale but do not establish loss scaling or downstream predictability.
record.test_reason: The paper's own results correlate a downstream capability score (PC1 of 12 benchmarks) with estimated training compute across about 21–27 open models. It also reports per-benchmark compute correlations. These results bear on V6, that downstream performance improves with scale, in a new cross-family observational setting. No loss, allocation or architecture results are reported, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors conclude that about half of AI safety benchmarks largely track general capabilities and training compute, which enables 'safetywashing'. They find that sycophancy and weaponization knowledge worsen with capabilities. They recommend reporting capabilities correlations and designing decorrelated benchmarks. They do not address loss-scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes cross-model rank correlations for capabilities and safety-benchmark scores, rather than fitting or testing power laws for held-out language-model loss or compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports separate analyses for base and chat models and notes that the capability-score correlation with compute is 93.7% for chat models and 96.5% for base models.
record.problems: The reported compute relationships are observational cross-model correlations, not controlled scaling experiments. Training compute estimates are unavailable for some models and are estimated for others; the paper does not report uncertainty for the correlations in these rows.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported results were extracted because the safety-benchmark correlations do not measure any version of the loss-scaling claim.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss and no power-law fits.
No extrapolation from small runs to larger ones.
No shape or architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Vision models are compared on ImageNet accuracy, not on loss scaling.
Predictability from pretraining loss, any functional form or quantitative forecast of downstream scores, and within-family controlled scaling.
No fitting choices or fit-dependence examined.

missing.what: Per-benchmark compute correlations for chat models. Positive: MT-Bench 79.8%, Chatbot Arena 61.5%, ETHICS 81.6%, TruthfulQA MC1 83.1%, GPQA 77.2%, QuALITY 91.6%, ANLI 86.1%, AdvGLUE 69.2%, AdvGLUE++ 48.5%. Weak or negative: BBQ Ambiguous −17.5%, CrowS-Pairs 2.8%, Discrim-Eval 34.2%, MACHIAVELLI −31.6%, sycophancy −66.8%, jailbreaks −9.2% to −22.5%. WMDP accuracy rises with compute (inverted score −83% to −91%).

record.verdict_notes: I override the reader's guess of discusses/T6. The compute–capability correlations (r1, r2) are the paper's own measurements of downstream performance against scale, so they bear on V6. The evidence is weak: observational, cross-family Spearman correlations with estimated FLOPs, no uncertainty reported and no fitted law. Most of the safety-benchmark correlations in the paper are against the capability score, not compute. Only the compute-correlation columns bear on V6 directly. The limits_scope label rests on text not captured in rows. Whether safety propensities count as 'downstream tasks' is debatable.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute; power-law form and range.
Fitting loss curves on small runs and testing predictions on substantially larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations, their growth with compute, and comparison of allocation trends.
Loss comparisons across depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream-task performance predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of loss-law fits or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices, or evidence of curves bending away from a single power law.

rows.subject: chat models
rows.operation_detail: Measured Spearman correlation between model capabilities scores and estimated training compute across models.

conditions.value: Training FLOPs; public estimates or estimates using 6 × Training Tokens × Params

rows.measure: Spearman correlation between capabilities score and log10(training FLOPs)
rows.locator: Figure 15 and Discussion, “The bitter lesson for AI safety research”
rows.note: Aggregate correlation across models; this measures capability scores, not held-out pretraining loss or a loss power law.
rows.check: Measures downstream capability (PC1 score of benchmarks) against estimated training FLOPs: Spearman 93.7% across chat models (Fig. 15). This is a rank correlation, not a fitted predictive law. Compute is estimated, partly by 6ND, for 21 of 26 chat models.

rows.subject: base models
rows.operation_detail: Measured Spearman correlation between model capabilities scores and estimated training compute across models.

conditions.value: Training FLOPs; public estimates or estimates using 6 × Training Tokens × Params

rows.measure: Spearman correlation between capabilities score and training compute
rows.locator: Discussion, “The bitter lesson for AI safety research”
rows.note: Aggregate correlation across base models; this measures capability scores, not held-out pretraining loss or a loss power law.
rows.check: Same measure for base models: Spearman 96.5%, stated in the Figure 15 caption. The number of base models with compute estimates is not stated.

relationships.condition: Composite capability score (PC1 of 12 standard benchmarks) vs estimated training compute, across open chat and base models
relationships.reason: Rank correlation with compute is 93.7% for chat models (r1) and 96.5% for base models (r2), i.e. a near-monotone improvement with scale.
relationships.display_finding: Capability scores had rank correlations with compute of 93.7% for chat models and 96.5% for base models.

relationships.condition: Safety and propensity benchmarks: jailbreak attacks, bias, MACHIAVELLI, sycophancy; chat models
relationships.reason: From the text, not rows. Compute correlations are weak or negative: Human Jailbreaks −15.2%, GCG −9.2%, CrowS-Pairs 2.8%, MACHIAVELLI −31.6%, sycophancy −66.8% (Tables 3, 4, 7).
relationships.display_finding: Compute correlations were −15.2% for Human Jailbreaks, −9.2% for GCG, 2.8% for CrowS-Pairs, −31.6% for MACHIAVELLI and −66.8% for sycophancy.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
